Vulnerability Management shows devices active in the last 30 days; software changes show in 2–4 hours (up to 8 on mobile), configuration changes in 4–24 hours.

keyTerms.definition: Frontline Defender for Endpoint capabilities, including network and web protection.
Intune integration type used to bring Defender for Endpoint device risk into compliance and app protection.
Defender for Endpoint risk level (Clear, Low, Medium, High) used in Intune compliance policies.
Uses onboarded endpoints to find unmanaged devices, network devices and IoT on corporate networks.
0–100 measure of how vulnerable the organization's devices are; lower is better.
Prioritized remediation step from Defender Vulnerability Management, actionable via Intune.

tables.title: Defender for Endpoint plans
rows: Next-gen protection, attack surface reduction, manual response actions, central management, security reports, APIs
Standalone, Windows 10/11 Enterprise E5/A5, Microsoft 365 E5/A5/G5, E5 Security
Plan 1 + device discovery, vulnerability management, threat analytics, AIR, advanced hunting, EDR, Threat Experts

tables.title: Device discovery modes
rows: Passive collection of network events seen by onboarded devices (SenseNDR.exe)
Passive + multicast discovery + smart active probing (Windows 10+/Server 2019+)

remember: Frontline of defense in the Defender for Endpoint stack → **attack surface reduction**.
Compliance risk level **Clear** = strictest, **High** = allows everything — don't invert them.
Block vulnerable apps for device groups → **remediation and tracking** in Defender Vulnerability Management.
Device discovery, vulnerability management and advanced hunting need **Plan 2**, not Plan 1.

selfCheck.q: A compromised laptop is rated High risk by Defender for Endpoint. How do you stop it reaching Exchange Online?
selfCheck.a: An Intune compliance policy with a lower allowed machine risk score marks it noncompliant, and a Conditional Access policy requiring a compliant device blocks access.

selfCheck.q: You want to find unpatched printers and unmanaged laptops on the corporate LAN. Which feature and mode?
selfCheck.a: Defender for Endpoint device discovery in Standard mode.

selfCheck.q: A recommendation can't be fixed yet because of a legacy app. What do you do?
selfCheck.a: File an exception with justification and duration from the recommendation's Exception options.

modules.title: Implement threat protection by using Microsoft Defender for Office 365
modules.learnSummary: This module examines the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 protection stack and its corresponding threat intelligence features, including Threat Explorer, Threat Trackers, and Attack simulation training. MS-102
modules.tldr: Microsoft Defender for Office 365 protects mail in four layers: edge protection, sender intelligence, content filtering and post-delivery protection. On top of preset and custom policies, Plan 2 gives SecOps Threat Explorer for investigation, Threat Trackers for trend intelligence, and Attack simulation training to find and educate vulnerable users.
objectives: Describe the protection stack provided by Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
Understand how Threat Explorer can be used to investigate threats and help to protect your tenant.
Describe the Threat Tracker widgets and views that provide you with intelligence on different cybersecurity issues that might affect your company.
Run realistic attack scenarios using Attack Simulator to help identify vulnerable users before a real attack impacts your organization.
keyPoints: Protection stack = **Edge protection** → **Sender intelligence** → **Content filtering** → **Post-delivery protection**; the exact path depends on configuration.
**Content filtering** checks message structure, word frequency, hyperlinks and attachments (mail flow rules, three AV engines, Safe Attachments, URL detonation).
**Post-delivery** covers Safe Links time-of-click, **ZAP** for phish/malware/spam, Campaign Views, Report Message add-ins and protection in SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams.
**Real-time detections** (Plan 1) is a subset of **Threat Explorer** (Plan 2); only Threat Explorer has the **All email** view, campaigns and remediation such as triggering AIR.
Explorer views default to **two days** of data, expandable to **30 days**; email list export up to **200,000** records. Multiple filters use AND unless switched to OR.
**Threat Trackers**: Noteworthy (threats Microsoft wants you to know), Trending (new in the past week, formerly Campaigns), Tracked queries (run automatically), Saved queries.
**Attack simulation training** needs Microsoft 365 E5 or Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 and Global Admin, Security Admin, **Attack Simulator Administrator** or **Payload Author** roles.
Simulation flow: **technique → payload → audience → training → launch**; compare actual vs **predicted compromise rate**.

units.title: Explore the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 protection stack
points: Edge (not the browser): network throttling, IP and domain reputation, directory-based edge filtering, backscatter detection, Enhanced Filtering for Connectors.

Sender intelligence: account compromise detection, email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ARC), intra-org and cross-domain spoof intelligence, bulk filtering, **mailbox intelligence** (communication graph), user and domain impersonation.

Content filtering: mail flow rules, Microsoft Defender Antivirus plus two third-party engines, common attachment filtering, attachment and URL reputation blocking, heuristic clustering, ML phishing models, Safe Attachments, linked content and URL detonation.
Post-delivery: Safe Links (also in Office apps), ZAP for phish/malware/spam, Campaign Views, Report Message/Report Phishing add-ins, Safe Attachments for OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams.

units.title: Examine the security policies and rules used in Microsoft Defender for Office 365
points: **Preset security policies** apply Microsoft-recommended settings for anti-phishing, anti-malware, Safe Attachments, Safe Links and anti-spam; assign them to users or groups.
**Custom policies**: threat policies, mail flow rules, outbound spam policies, and Defender for Office 365 anti-phishing (impersonation), Safe Attachments and Safe Links policies.
Advanced features (Attack Simulator, Threat Explorer, Threat Trackers, threat intelligence, Threat protection status report) require Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 or Microsoft 365 E5.

units.title: Investigate security attacks by using Threat Explorer
points: Threat Explorer lets analysts see malware and phish detections, URL click verdicts, email timeline, header preview, delivered malicious mail, and malicious files in SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams.
Views: **All email** (Explorer default, Explorer only), **Malware** (Real-time detections default), **Phish**, **Content malware** (OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams).
Components: filters, charts, results grid (UTC or local time), detail panes for email, recipient, IP and URL; actions such as Delete an email.
The Threat Dashboard gives executives a broad view; Explorer gives analysts the drill-down.

units.title: Identify cybersecurity issues by using Threat Trackers
points: Defender portal → Email & collaboration → Threat tracker; requires Global Administrator, Security Administrator or Security Reader.
Noteworthy trackers stay posted only a couple of weeks (e.g. WannaCry, Petya); Trending trackers show threats new to your mail in the past week.
Save Explorer queries with **Save query**; tracked queries rerun automatically for trending. Trackers link to Threat Explorer for details.
Noteworthy items include new malicious files found by Safe Attachments; the **Advanced Analysis** tab (detonation details) exists only for Safe Attachments detections.

units.title: Prepare for attacks with Attack simulation training
points: Runs benign simulations to find vulnerable users and train them; on-premises mailboxes are supported with reduced reporting.
Techniques: credential harvest, malware attachment, link in attachment, link to malware, drive-by URL (watering hole).
Payload data points: click rate, predicted compromise rate, simulations launched, complexity, source (tenant or global).
Target all or specific users (search or CSV import), assign training with a due date, schedule with region-aware time zone delivery and an end time.
End-user notifications: positive reinforcement, simulation, training assignment and training reminder; global (built-in) vs tenant (custom).

keyTerms.definition: First stack layer of automatic edge blocks (throttling, reputation, directory harvest and backscatter protection).
Learns each user's communication graph to detect senders impersonating usual contacts.
Plan 2 hunting and remediation tool for email and collaboration threats; Real-time detections is its Plan 1 subset.
Widgets and views (Noteworthy, Trending, Tracked and Saved queries) giving intelligence on threats.
Plan 2 / E5 feature for benign phishing simulations with assigned training.
Average compromise rate for the same payload type across other tenants, compared with your actual rate.

tables.title: Defender for Office 365 protection stack
rows: IP/domain reputation, network throttling, backscatter detection, Enhanced Filtering
SPF/DKIM/DMARC/ARC, spoof intelligence, mailbox intelligence, impersonation protection
Mail flow rules, AV engines, Safe Attachments, URL reputation, ML models
After delivery, across Teams and Office
Safe Links, ZAP, Campaign Views, Report Message add-ins

tables.title: Threat Explorer vs Real-time detections
rows: Campaign details and remediation (e.g. trigger AIR)

remember: Message structure, word frequency, links and attachments → **content filtering layer**, not edge or post-delivery.
Threats Microsoft thinks you should know about → **Noteworthy trackers**; new to your tenant this week → **Trending trackers**.
Only Threat Explorer has the **All email** view — if you only see Malware/Phish views, you're on **Plan 1**.
Attack simulation training needs **E5 or Defender for Office 365 Plan 2**.

selfCheck.q: Analysts need to find every delivered message from a malicious campaign and delete it from mailboxes. Which tool?
selfCheck.a: Threat Explorer (Plan 2), using the All email or Phish view and the Delete an email remediation action.

selfCheck.q: You want to test whether users enter passwords on a fake sign-in page. Which simulation technique?
selfCheck.a: Credential harvest.

selfCheck.q: Which stack layer stops directory harvest attempts over SMTP?
selfCheck.a: The edge protection layer (directory-based edge filtering).

paths.title: MS-102 Explore data governance in Microsoft 365
paths.summary: This learning path introduces you to the data governance features of Microsoft 365, which serve regulatory compliance, can facilitate eDiscovery, and are part of a business strategy to protect the integrity of the data estate.

modules.title: Examine data governance solutions in Microsoft Purview
modules.learnSummary: This module introduces Microsoft Purview, which is designed to meet the challenges of today’s decentralized, data-rich workplace by providing a comprehensive set of solutions that help organizations govern, protect, and manage their entire data estate. MS-102
modules.tldr: Microsoft Purview is Microsoft's unified data governance and compliance service, built on three pillars: data governance, eDiscovery and auditing. This module tours four of its solutions: Information Protection (know, protect and prevent loss of sensitive data), Data Lifecycle Management (keep what you need, delete what you don't), Insider Risk Management (detect and act on risky internal activity) and the three eDiscovery tiers.
objectives: Protect sensitive data with Microsoft Purview Information Protection.
Govern organizational data using Microsoft Purview Data Lifecycle Management.
Minimize internal risks with Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management.
Explain the Microsoft Purview eDiscovery solutions.
keyPoints: Purview rests on three pillars: **data governance** (import, store, preserve, retire and expire data), **eDiscovery** (find relevant information fast) and **auditing** (monitor and investigate actions on data).

The **Data Map** captures metadata through automated scanning and classification; it powers the **Data Catalog** (search, glossary, lineage) and **Data Estate Insights** (where sensitive data is and how it moves).
Registering a data source copies only its **metadata** and a reference into Purview — the **data stays where it is**.
Information Protection follows three steps: **know your data** (sensitive info types, trainable classifiers), **protect your data** (sensitivity labels, encryption) and **prevent data loss** (DLP).
**Retention policies** are the cornerstone of Data Lifecycle Management; **retention labels** handle exceptions for individual items. Use records management for high-value records.

**Insider Risk Management** policies are built from **templates** that define triggering events and indicators (max five policies per template); workflow: policies → alerts → triage → investigate → action.

eDiscovery has three tiers: **Content search** (search + export), **eDiscovery (Standard)** (adds cases and legal hold) and **eDiscovery (Premium)** (adds custodians, review sets, analytics; needs E5).

units.title: Explore data governance and compliance in Microsoft Purview
points: Organizations struggle to know what data they have, where it is and what it's doing; Purview addresses preserving data, finding it, and auditing/monitoring activity.
Purview governs on-premises, multicloud and SaaS data with automated discovery, sensitive data classification and end-to-end lineage.
**Data Map**: cloud-native PaaS that captures metadata, kept current by automated scanning; developers can use Apache Atlas 2.2 APIs.

**Data Catalog**: search with filters (glossary terms, classifications, sensitivity labels), glossary management and visual lineage. **Data Estate Insights**: high-level view of scanned data, sensitive data locations and data movement.
Registration adds a copy of metadata plus a reference; users can enrich it with descriptions, tags and access-request information.

units.title: Protect sensitive data with Microsoft Purview Information Protection
points: **Know your data**: sensitive information types (patterns, keywords, confidence, proximity), trainable classifiers (learn from examples) and data classification (content explorer, activity explorer).

**Protect your data**: sensitivity labels across apps, services and devices; Double Key Encryption (only your organization can decrypt), Office 365 Message Encryption, Customer Key, SharePoint IRM, the on-premises scanner and Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps for cloud data stores.
**Prevent data loss**: DLP policies, extended to Windows 10+ endpoints, Chrome (Microsoft Compliance Extension), on-premises file shares and Teams chat/channel messages.
Licensing depends on the scenarios and features used, not a fixed license per capability.

units.title: Govern organizational data using Microsoft Purview Data Lifecycle Management
points: Retention policies cover Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and Viva Engage; typical setting: retain then delete (e.g. keep email three years, then delete). Scope: all instances or specific ones.
Retention labels create exceptions for individual items, applied by users or automatically; use records management for high-value records.
Other capabilities: **mailbox archiving** (auto-expanding archiving beyond 100 GB), **inactive mailboxes** (keep content after employees leave) and **PST import** (network upload or drive shipping).

Permissions: Compliance Administrator role group, or a custom group with Retention Management (View-Only Retention Management for read-only). Configuring policies doesn't require access to the content.
Retention policies work in the background; retention labels appear in apps, so users and help desk need guidance.

units.title: Minimize internal risks with Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management
points: Detects risks such as data leaks, confidentiality violations, IP theft, fraud and insider trading, using Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Graph logs. Principles: transparency (privacy by design), configurable, integrated, actionable.
**Insider risk analytics** evaluates potential risks without configuring any policies; **recommended actions** guide initial setup.

Templates define triggering events and prerequisites — e.g. *Data theft by departing users* uses HR connector resignation/termination dates; *Security policy violations* need Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
Alerts start as **Needs review**; triage by opening a case, adding to an existing case or dismissing. Cases offer user activity charts, content explorer and case notes.
Actions: reminder notices to users, escalate to **eDiscovery (Premium)**, or export alerts to a SIEM via the Office 365 Management APIs.

units.title: Explore Microsoft Purview eDiscovery solutions
points: eDiscovery identifies and delivers electronic information used as evidence in legal cases.
**Content search**: search Microsoft 365 data sources with KQL, view statistics and export results (copied to Microsoft-provided Azure Storage, then downloaded).
**eDiscovery (Standard)** adds cases (managers only see their own cases) and holds on content locations.

**eDiscovery (Premium)** (Office 365 E5 / Microsoft 365 E5 or add-on) adds custodian management, legal hold notifications, advanced indexing, error remediation, review sets, OCR, conversation threading, tagging, analytics (near duplicates, email threading, themes) and predictive coding.
Premium can export to a customer-owned Azure Storage account.

keyTerms.definition: Cloud-native PaaS that captures metadata about enterprise data through automated scanning and classification.
Identifies sensitive content from examples of that content instead of pattern matching.
Item-level retention setting used for exceptions to a retention policy; applied manually or automatically.
Predefined policy conditions that set the risk indicators, triggering events and risk scoring model for a policy.
A person of interest in an eDiscovery (Premium) case whose data sources are held and collected.
Secure Microsoft-provided Azure Storage location in eDiscovery (Premium) where collected items are copied for search, tagging and analysis.
Encryption where only your organization can ever decrypt protected content.

tables.title: eDiscovery tiers
rows: Review sets, tagging, analytics, predictive coding, OCR

remember: Need **cases and holds** but no custodians → **eDiscovery (Standard)**; custodians, notifications, review sets → **eDiscovery (Premium)**.
Mailbox over **100 GB** → enable **auto-expanding archiving**, not a new retention policy.
Retention policy = broad, background, per location; retention **label** = item-level **exception** that users see.
Departing-user data theft template → needs the **HR connector** for resignation/termination dates.

selfCheck.q: Legal wants to send hold notifications to employees involved in a case and track who acknowledged them. Which tool?
selfCheck.a: eDiscovery (Premium) — custodian management and legal hold notifications are Premium-only.

selfCheck.q: Most email must be kept three years, but legal contracts must be kept longer. How do you configure this?
selfCheck.a: A retention policy for the mailbox workload (retain three years, then delete) plus a retention label with a longer period for the contracts as the exception.

selfCheck.q: A user's activity matched an insider risk policy. What can a reviewer do with the alert during triage?
selfCheck.a: Open a new case, add the alert to an existing case, or dismiss it.

modules.title: Explore data management practices in Microsoft 365
modules.learnSummary: This module examines how Microsoft 365 supports data governance by enabling organizations to archive content by using archive mailboxes and restore deleted data in Exchange Online and SharePoint Online.
modules.tldr: Archive mailboxes give users extra storage inside Exchange Online instead of local .pst files, and stay covered by compliance features such as Content search, retention and Litigation Hold. When data is deleted, Exchange Online recovers it through the Recoverable Items folder and single item recovery, while SharePoint Online uses a two-stage recycle bin with a fixed 93-day retention.
objectives: Enable and disable an archive mailbox in the Microsoft Purview portal and through Windows PowerShell.
Run diagnostic tests on an archive mailbox.
Restore deleted data in Exchange Online and SharePoint Online.
keyPoints: Enabling archiving creates a separate **archive mailbox** next to the **primary** mailbox; both count as the user's mailbox for Content search, retention and **Litigation Hold**.
The **default retention policy** moves items **two years** or older to the archive, and Recoverable Items older than **14 days** to the archive's Recoverable Items folder.
An archive gives **100 GB** extra; **auto-expanding archiving** raises this to **1.5 TB**. The archive is **not cached** in Outlook cached mode, so it needs a connection to Exchange.
A disabled archive can be **reconnected within 30 days**; after that its content is permanently deleted and re-enabling creates a new, empty archive.
Exchange Online keeps soft-deleted items **14 days by default (max 30)**; **single item recovery** is on by default, so admins can still recover hard-deleted items within that period.
Restoring email is two steps: **recover** to a discovery mailbox (EAC or `Get-RecoverableItems`), then **restore** with `Restore-RecoverableItems` — PowerShell only.

SharePoint keeps deleted items **93 days** across the **site (first-stage)** and **site collection (second-stage)** recycle bins; not configurable. Backups exist **14 more days** via Microsoft Support.

units.title: Explore archive mailboxes in Microsoft 365
points: Archive mailboxes replace user-managed .pst files; users fill them by drag and drop, an archive policy or importing a .pst.

The **Recoverable Items** folder (formerly *the dumpster*) sits in the hidden non-IPM subtree; it has its own quota, is indexed for eDiscovery and supports single item recovery, holds and audit logging.
Delete → Deleted Items → Recoverable Items; **Shift+Delete** goes straight to Recoverable Items.
Default retention policy: items 2+ years old move to the archive; Recoverable Items 14+ days old move to the archive's Recoverable Items.
Searching the entire mailbox returns results from both primary and archive; auto-expanding archiving gives up to 1.5 TB.

units.title: Enable archive mailboxes in Microsoft 365
points: Requires the **Mail Recipients** role (in Recipient Management and Organization Management role groups by default).
EAC: select the mailbox → **Others** → **Manage mailbox archive** → toggle to Enabled; status shows **Active**.
PowerShell (best for all users at once): `Enable-Mailbox -Identity <user> -Archive` / `Disable-Mailbox -Identity <user> -Archive`.
Disabling leaves items in the primary mailbox; reconnect within 30 days or the archive content is lost.
Diagnostics: Microsoft 365 admin center **Help** → search **Diag: Archive Mailbox** → Run Tests (Global Administrator required).

units.title: Restore deleted data in Exchange Online
points: **Soft deletion**: item goes to Recoverable Items\Deletions. **Hard deletion**: user purges it with Recover Deleted Items.
Deleted item retention is 14 days by default, up to 30 days; single item recovery is enabled by default in Exchange Online (disabled by default in Exchange Server).
Admins can recover items purged by users or by automated processes such as retention policies, as long as the retention period hasn't expired.
Needed: source mailbox, target (discovery) mailbox and search criteria. Recover via EAC (**Recover deleted items**) or `Get-RecoverableItems`; restore only via `Restore-RecoverableItems`.

units.title: Restore deleted data in SharePoint Online
points: Deleted items stay in the **Site recycle bin** for 93 days; if deleted or emptied from there, they move to the **Site Collection recycle bin** for the remainder of the 93 days.
Users with edit permissions can restore their own and others' items; the second-stage bin needs administrator or owner permissions.

Restoring a container (list, library, folder) brings back its content; you can't restore an item whose parent (e.g. library) is deleted without restoring the parent first — except items from folders, where the folder is recreated.
Site Collection recycle bin space is 200% of the site collection quota; deleted site collections are kept 93 days and can be restored by a Global or SharePoint Administrator.
Hard deletion: purge from the second-stage bin, retention expiry, or `Remove-SPODeletedSite`.

keyTerms.definition: Secondary mailbox for extra storage, shown in Outlook and Outlook on the web, covered by the same compliance features as the primary mailbox.
Extends archive storage beyond 100 GB, up to 1.5 TB.
Hidden folder in the non-IPM subtree that holds deleted items and supports single item recovery, holds and auditing.
Lets admins recover hard-deleted items until the deleted item retention period expires; on by default in Exchange Online.
Target mailbox where recovered items are placed before they are restored.
The SharePoint Site Collection recycle bin, holding items deleted from the site recycle bin for the rest of the 93 days.

tables.title: Deleted data retention at a glance
rows: EAC or Get-RecoverableItems to recover; Restore-RecoverableItems to restore

remember: Restore recovered email → **PowerShell only** (`Restore-RecoverableItems`); the EAC can only recover.
Exchange **14 days (max 30)** vs SharePoint **93 days (fixed)** — don't mix them up.
Archive not available offline in cached mode → the archive is **never cached**, by design.
Enable archives for **all users** at once → PowerShell `Get-Mailbox ... | Enable-Mailbox -Archive`.

selfCheck.q: An admin disabled a user's archive 45 days ago and now re-enables it. What does the user get?
selfCheck.a: A new, empty archive mailbox — the original archive content was permanently deleted after 30 days.

selfCheck.q: A retention policy purged messages from a mailbox last week. Can they be recovered?
selfCheck.a: Yes, if single item recovery was enabled and the deleted item retention period hasn't expired: recover them to a discovery mailbox, then restore with Restore-RecoverableItems.

selfCheck.q: A user deleted a file and then emptied the site recycle bin. Where can it still be restored?
selfCheck.a: From the Site Collection (second-stage) recycle bin by a site collection administrator, within the remainder of the 93 days.

modules.title: Explore retention in Microsoft 365
modules.learnSummary: This module examines how data can be retained and ultimately removed in Microsoft 365 by using data retention policies and data retention labels in retention policies. MS-102
modules.tldr: Retention in Microsoft 365 keeps content in place and can retain-only, delete-only, or retain and then delete it. Retention policies apply settings broadly at container level; retention labels work per item, travel with the content and add features such as records, event-based retention and disposition review. When settings conflict, the four principles of retention decide the outcome, and Preservation Lock stops anyone from weakening a policy.
objectives: Explain how a retention policies and retention labels work.
Identify the capabilities of both retention policies and retention labels.
Select the appropriate scope for a policy depending on business requirements.
Explain the principles of retention.
Identify the differences between retention settings and eDiscovery holds.
Restrict retention changes by using preservation lock.
keyPoints: Retained content stays **in place**; when edited or deleted, a copy is kept in the **Preservation Hold library** (SharePoint/OneDrive), **Recoverable Items** (Exchange) or **SubstrateHolds** (Teams and Viva Engage).

**Retention policies** assign settings at **container level**; **retention labels** work at **item level**, persist when content moves within the tenant, and support records, event-based start, disposition review and auto-apply conditions.
An item can have **only one retention label** but **several retention policies**.

Principles of retention: 1) **retention wins over deletion**, 2) **longest retention wins**, 3) **explicit wins over implicit** (label delete beats policy delete; scoped policy beats org-wide), 4) **shortest deletion wins**.
**Adaptive scopes** use attribute queries that run daily; **static scopes** are org-wide, includes or excludes. Public folders need static; adaptive scopes don't support Preservation Lock.
**eDiscovery holds** are short-term, legal, user-based and never auto-delete — they always take precedence over retention settings.
**Preservation Lock** (Security & Compliance PowerShell only, `-RestrictiveRetention $true`) prevents anyone, even Global Administrators, from disabling, deleting or weakening a policy.
Policies and auto-applied labels can take **up to seven days** to take effect; retry distribution with `Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy -RetryDistribution`.

units.title: Explore retention by using retention policies and retention labels
points: Two actions — retain and delete — give three outcomes: retain-only, delete-only, retain then delete.
Use a policy for one setting across a site or mailbox; use labels when items in the same location need different settings (e.g. five vs. ten years).

Labels can be applied manually, auto-applied (sensitive info types, keywords/queries, trainable classifiers, cloud attachments) or as a default label on a library, folder or document set; they can also mark items as a record or be used as a DLP condition.
Exchange public folders, Skype, Teams and Viva Engage messages don't support retention labels — use retention policies.
If several auto-apply policies match, the **oldest** auto-apply policy wins; use **Policy lookup** with an exact email address or site URL to find applied policies.

units.title: Compare capabilities in retention policies and retention labels
points: Only labels offer manual application, end-user interaction, records, disposition review, proof of disposition (up to seven years) and applying a different label at the end of the period.
Combine both: e.g. a policy deletes OneDrive content after five years, while a published "keep forever" label lets users exempt specific documents.
Policies and auto-applied labels can take up to seven days to apply.
On a distribution error, retry with `Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy -RetryDistribution` (or `Set-AppRetentionCompliancePolicy` for Teams private channels and Viva Engage).

units.title: Define the scope of a retention policy
points: **Adaptive scope**: query on attributes (e.g. Entra ID job title "Executive") that runs daily, so new users are picked up automatically.
**Static scope**: org-wide, includes or excludes; you must maintain groups and OneDrive URLs yourself (URLs change with the UPN).
Adaptive advantages: no item limit per policy, attribute-based targeting, Teams and Viva Engage in one policy, and the only way to target inactive mailboxes.
Static is simpler when all instances are selected and is required for Exchange and Skype for Business public folders. Adaptive scopes don't support Preservation Lock.

units.title: Examine the principles of retention
points: The outcome is how long an item is retained and when it's deleted — calculated independently, not which single policy wins.
Levels act as tie-breakers top to bottom: retention over deletion → longest retention → explicit over implicit for deletion → shortest deletion.
Retention normally starts at creation date; for files it can start at last modified (resets on each edit); labels can also start when labeled or at an event.
Items under eDiscovery hold can't be permanently deleted by any policy or label until the hold is released.

units.title: Implement retention using retention policies, retention labels, and eDiscovery holds
points: Retention = compliance, long-term, broad and content-based, configurable dates, optional deletion, low overhead.
eDiscovery holds = legal, short-term, user-based, not configurable, no deletion, high overhead.
Microsoft recommends retention policies and labels over older features: MRM retention tags, Litigation Hold, SharePoint document deletion and information management policies.
MRM is still needed for archive policies (moving mail to the archive) and admin-set folder-level retention; older features keep working side by side.

units.title: Restrict retention changes by using Preservation Lock
points: Meets rules such as **SEC Rule 17a-4** and guards against rogue administrators.
Locked retention policy: can't disable or delete; can add (not remove) locations; can extend (not shorten) retention.
Locked label policy: can add locations and labels but not remove them — it doesn't stop an admin from shortening a label's period (use a regulatory record for that).
Only via Security & Compliance PowerShell: `Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy -Identity "<name>" -RestrictiveRetention $true`; verify with `Get-RetentionCompliancePolicy ... | Fl`.

keyTerms.definition: Applies retain and/or delete settings to a whole location (container); items inherit them.
Item-level retention setting that travels with content within the tenant; one label per item.
Hidden SharePoint/OneDrive library that keeps original copies of retained content that's edited or deleted.
Query-based, dynamic policy scope evaluated daily against user, site or group attributes.
Policy scope set as org-wide, includes or excludes of specific instances.
Label option to review content before it's permanently deleted at the end of retention.
Lock on a retention (label) policy so nobody can disable, delete or make it less restrictive.

tables.title: Retention policy vs. retention label
rows: Teams, Viva Engage, Skype, public folders
Start when labeled or on an event

remember: Delete-after-3-years policy + retain-5-years label → kept **5 years**, then deleted: **retention beats deletion**.
Org-wide policy deletes after 5 years, scoped policy after 3 → deleted after **3 years** (scoped/explicit wins at level 3).
Preservation Lock → **PowerShell only**, irreversible, and **not** with adaptive scopes.
Need different periods inside one library → **labels**, not policies.

selfCheck.q: Executives' mail and OneDrive need longer retention, and new executives must be covered automatically. Which scope?
selfCheck.a: An adaptive scope querying the Entra ID job title attribute — it re-evaluates daily, so new executives are added without editing the policy.

selfCheck.q: A document has two retention policies deleting after 5 and 10 years and a label deleting after 7 years. When is it deleted?
selfCheck.a: After seven years — a delete action from a retention label takes precedence over delete actions from retention policies.

selfCheck.q: A broker must ensure no admin can ever shorten or disable its retention policy. What do you configure?
selfCheck.a: Preservation Lock, via Security & Compliance PowerShell with Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy -RestrictiveRetention $true.

paths.title: MS-102 Implement compliance in Microsoft 365
paths.summary: This learning path provides instruction on implementing the Microsoft 365 data governance features, including how to calculate your compliance readiness, implement compliance solutions, and create information barriers, DLP policies, and policy tips.

modules.title: Explore compliance in Microsoft 365
modules.learnSummary: This module explores the tools Microsoft 365 provides to help ensure an organization's regulatory compliance, including the Microsoft Purview compliance portal, Compliance Manager, and the Microsoft compliance score. MS-102
modules.tldr: Security and compliance in Microsoft 365 is a shared responsibility: Microsoft protects the services, you protect your data, identities and devices. The module gives an eight-task starter plan for Microsoft Purview (permissions, compliance posture, auditing, alerts, labels, retention, communication compliance, explorers). It then explains how Compliance Manager uses controls, assessments, templates and improvement actions to produce a risk-based compliance score.
objectives: Describe how Microsoft 365 helps organizations manage risks, protect data, and remain compliant with regulations and standards.
Plan your beginning compliance tasks in Microsoft Purview.
Manage your compliance requirements with Compliance Manager.
Manage compliance posture and improvement actions using the Compliance Manager dashboard.
Explain how an organization's compliance score is determined.
keyPoints: Planning order: review capabilities → **check Secure Score** → plan identity and device access protection → plan data protection by sensitivity → use the **Microsoft Purview portal** → start from end-to-end scenarios.
First Purview task: **assign compliance permissions** (Compliance administrator, Compliance data administrator; **Global Reader** to view Compliance Manager data).
**Auditing** must be on before activities are recorded; logs are kept **180 days**, up to one year depending on license.
Compliance Manager's initial score comes from the **Microsoft 365 data protection baseline** (drawing on NIST CSF, ISO and FedRAMP).
Hierarchy: **controls** (requirements; Microsoft-managed, yours, or shared) → grouped in **assessments** → built from **templates** (300+ prebuilt) → fulfilled through **improvement actions**.
Only actions with test status **Passed** count toward the score; status updates within **24 hours** of a change.
**Technical** actions score once per tenant; **nontechnical** actions score **once per group**.
Point values: preventative mandatory **27**, preventative discretionary **9**, detective/corrective mandatory **3**, detective/corrective discretionary **1**.

units.title: Plan for security and compliance in Microsoft 365
points: Security is a partnership: the organization protects data, identities and devices; Microsoft protects the Microsoft 365 services.
Six planning steps, with Secure Score as the starting baseline right after setting up the subscription.

Security and compliance settings live in the Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft Purview, Exchange/SharePoint/OneDrive admin centers, Microsoft Entra ID, Intune and Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps.

units.title: Plan your beginning compliance tasks in Microsoft Purview
points: Tasks 1–4: configure compliance permissions, know your compliance state (Compliance Manager), enable auditing (180 days, up to one year), and use/customize alert policies (built-in ones are on by default).
Task 5: sensitivity labels for encryption, usage restrictions and visual markings. Task 6: retention policies, scoped adaptively or statically.
Task 7: communication compliance templates — **Offensive language and anti-harassment** and **Sensitive information** — for email, Teams, Viva Engage and third-party communications.
Task 8: **Content explorer** shows labeled/classified items in native format; **Activity explorer** shows what users did with them (30+ filters).

units.title: Manage your compliance requirements with Compliance Manager
points: Helps inventory data protection risks, implement controls, stay current with regulations and report to auditors.
Assessments must be assigned to a **group** (e.g. by audit year, region or team); the dashboard can be filtered per group.
A free **90-day premium assessments trial** recommends templates based on your industry and region.

**Automated testing** uses signals from other Purview solutions and Secure Score; it's on by default and data takes about seven days to collect. Only a Global Administrator can toggle it for all actions; a Compliance Manager Administrator can enable it per action.
**Manage user history**: export a report, reassign improvement actions, or permanently delete a user's history.

units.title: Examine the Compliance Manager dashboard
points: Dashboard: overall compliance score, key improvement actions, solutions that affect your score, and a breakdown by category and assessment. Filters adjust the score in real time and persist after sign-out.
Improvement actions tab hides **Passed** actions by default; statuses include Not assessed, Failed (low/medium/high risk), Out of scope, To be detected and Partially tested.
Solutions tab shows earned vs. potential points per solution; Assessments tab statuses: Complete, Incomplete, None, In progress.
Adding assessments increases the score **denominator** and the number of improvement actions.
Alerts and Alert policies tabs let you assign, email and manage alerts and their policies.

units.title: Analyze the Microsoft Compliance score
points: Scores exist at three levels: improvement action, control (counts when Implemented/Alternative Implementation and Passed) and assessment.
Example: a 3-point action in five groups gives 3 points if technical, 15 points if nontechnical.
Actions are **mandatory** (can't be bypassed, e.g. password policy) or **discretionary** (relies on users), and **preventative**, **detective** or **corrective**.
Compliance Manager detects settings automatically — e.g. enabling MFA in the Microsoft Entra admin center updates the related action, usually the next day.

keyTerms.definition: A requirement of a regulation, standard or policy; Microsoft-managed, customer-managed or shared.
A grouping of controls for one regulation or standard (e.g. ISO 27001), assigned to a group.
Framework for creating an assessment; prebuilt or custom.
Recommended step, assignable to a user, that earns points when implemented and tested as Passed.
Default assessment that sets the initial compliance score, drawing on NIST CSF, ISO and FedRAMP.
Shows actions users took on labeled and classified items across SharePoint, Exchange and OneDrive.

remember: Initial compliance score → **data protection baseline**, not your own assessments.
Technical action = points **once**; nontechnical = points **per group**.
Requirement of a regulation (config, process, people) → a **control**, not an assessment.
After setting up the subscription, the next planning step is to **check Secure Score**.

selfCheck.q: A user must view data in Compliance Manager without changing anything. Which role do you assign?
selfCheck.a: The Microsoft Entra Global Reader role.

selfCheck.q: A nontechnical action worth 9 points exists in three assessment groups and is completed in all three. How many points?
selfCheck.a: 27 — nontechnical actions score once per group.

selfCheck.q: Why does adding a new ISO assessment lower the compliance score percentage at first?
selfCheck.a: Tracked assessments set the score denominator; more assessments add more possible points and improvement actions.

modules.title: Implement Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management
modules.learnSummary: This module examines how Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management helps organizations minimize internal risks by enabling them to detect, investigate, and act on malicious and inadvertent activities. MS-102
modules.tldr: Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management detects, investigates and acts on risky activity by your own users, such as data theft, leaks and security policy violations. You build policies from templates with triggering events and indicators. Alerts are triaged into cases, and a case ends with a notice to the user, a resolution, or escalation to eDiscovery (Premium).
objectives: Describe insider risk management functionality in Microsoft 365.
Develop a plan to implement the Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management solution.
Create insider risk management policies.
Manage insider risk management alerts and cases.
keyPoints: Workflow: **policies → alerts → triage → investigate → action**. **Cases** are the heart of the solution and are scoped to a **single user**.
**Analytics** scans for potential insider risks **without any policies** (results within 48 hours) to help pick the right policies.
Each policy needs a **template**; up to **five policies per template**. A user is only scored after a **triggering event** (or after being added manually).

Prerequisites per template: **HR connector** (departing or disgruntled users), a **DLP policy with High severity alerts** (data leaks), **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** integration (security violations), **priority user groups** (priority users).

**Priority content** (SharePoint sites, sensitive info types, sensitivity labels, up to 50 file extensions) raises risk scores; **sequence detection** links collection → exfiltration → obfuscation → clean-up.
Role groups split duties: Admin configures, **Analysts** handle alerts and cases, **Investigators** also see **Content explorer**, **Auditors** view audit logs. Keep at least one admin.
Test with a **small group of production users** with **anonymization** turned on.
Resolve a case as **Benign** or **Confirmed policy violation**; sending a notice does **not** close the case.

units.title: Explore insider risk management
points: Targets internal risks: data leaks, confidentiality violations, IP theft, fraud, insider trading, regulatory violations; uses Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Graph logs.
Principles: transparency (privacy by design), configurable, integrated, actionable.
Enable analytics via **Run scan** (Insider Risk Management, Insider Risk Management Admin or Global Administrator role); insights take up to 48 hours.
**Recommended actions** on the Overview tab: turn on auditing, get permissions, choose indicators, scan, assign permissions, create your first policy.
Actions after investigation: reminder notices, escalate to eDiscovery (Premium), or export alerts to a SIEM via Office 365 Management APIs.

units.title: Plan for insider risk management
points: Involve stakeholders from IT, compliance, privacy, security, HR and legal; separate policies per region or division can involve the right reviewers.
Global Administrator, Compliance Administrator and Organization Management can assign users to the insider risk role groups.
Requires appropriate licensing (e.g. Microsoft 365 E5 or a trial) and a supported Azure region.
If no alerts appear, the minimum risk threshold may not be met — check on the **Users** page that the user is in scope.

units.title: Explore insider risk management policies
points: Policies define in-scope users, risk indicators, priority content, risk score boosters and the policy window.
Policies tab shows health status, active and confirmed alerts, and **policy alert effectiveness** (confirmed alerts ÷ actions taken).
Data theft by departing users uses the HR connector **or** the *User account deleted from Microsoft Entra ID* trigger.
Data leaks templates: only DLP rules with **Incident reports = High** trigger; users must be in scope in **both** the DLP and the insider risk policy; one DLP policy per insider risk policy.
Patient data misuse needs the Microsoft Healthcare or Epic connector plus the HR connector.

units.title: Create insider risk management policies
points: Wizard: template → name (can't change later) → users and groups (no guest accounts) → priority content → triggers → indicators → thresholds → review.
Indicators must first be enabled in **Settings > Policy indicators** before a policy can use them.
Sequence detection (data theft and data leaks templates) tracks collection, exfiltration, obfuscation and clean-up activity.
**Start scoring activity for users** adds users manually for 5–30 days, bypassing the triggering event (e.g. after a tip or before the HR connector is ready).

units.title: Investigate insider risk management activities and alerts
points: **User activity reports** show a user's activity for up to 90 days without a policy or triggering event; they need the Investigators role and take up to 10 hours to build.
Alert statuses: Needs review, Confirmed, Dismissed, Resolved. Severity (High/Medium/Low) comes from the risk score, can't be customized, and can rise if left untriaged.
**Alert throttling** protects against alert overload, for example from misconfigured connectors or DLP policies.
Activity explorer filters by scope and risk factors such as unusual activity, priority content, sequences and cumulative exfiltration.

units.title: Explore insider risk management cases
points: Case tabs: overview (risk score recalculated every 24 hours), alerts, user activity, activity explorer, content explorer, case notes and contributors.
Case notes are permanent — they can't be edited or deleted.
Contributors get case access but can't confirm/dismiss alerts, edit contributors or open Content explorer.
Actions: send email notice (case stays open), escalate for investigation (creates an eDiscovery (Premium) case), or resolve as Benign / Confirmed policy violation.

keyTerms.definition: Event that brings a user into scope for risk scoring, such as an HR resignation date or a High severity DLP alert.
A user activity the organization wants to detect; enabled globally in settings, then selected per policy.
Group of higher-risk users (e.g. executives, admins) defined in settings for priority-user templates.
Links related activities (collection, exfiltration, obfuscation, clean-up) into one higher-risk sequence.
Per-user view of up to 90 days of risky activity, available without a policy or alert.
Built-in limit that prevents an overload of alerts and may delay new alerts for a user.

tables.title: Template prerequisites at a glance
rows: Resignation/termination date or Entra ID account deletion
High severity DLP alert or exfiltration indicators
DLP policy with High incident reports; priority user groups for priority variant
Performance or job level change from HR
HR connector (plus Defender for Endpoint for security)
Defense evasion or unwanted software detected
Healthcare or Epic connector + HR connector

remember: Heart of the workflow → **cases**, not alerts.
Data leaks policy shows no alerts → check the DLP rule's **Incident reports** setting is **High** and the users are in scope in both policies.
Need to see files and messages in a case → **Insider Risk Management Investigators** role; Analysts can't.
Max **5 policies per template**.

selfCheck.q: HR tips you off about an employee before any trigger has fired. How do you start scoring their activity?
selfCheck.a: Use Start scoring activity for users on the Policies tab to add them manually for 5–30 days, or create a user activity report.

selfCheck.q: You want a departing-users policy but have no HR connector. What trigger can you use?
selfCheck.a: The User account deleted from Microsoft Entra ID option.

selfCheck.q: An investigation needs legal hold and custodian management. What do you do with the insider risk case?
selfCheck.a: Escalate for investigation, which creates an eDiscovery (Premium) case.

modules.title: Implement Microsoft Purview Information Barriers
modules.learnSummary: This module examines how Microsoft Purview uses information barriers to restrict communication and collaboration in Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, and OneDrive for Business. MS-102
modules.tldr: Microsoft Purview Information Barriers (IB) put two-way limits on communication and collaboration between groups of users in Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive, for example to prevent conflicts of interest in financial services. You group users into segments based on directory attributes, define block or allow policies, and apply them. IB modes (Open, Implicit, Explicit, Owner Moderated, Inferred) then control who can access and share each team, site or OneDrive.
objectives: Describe how information barriers can restrict or allow communication and collaboration among specific groups of users.
Describe the components of an information barrier and how to enable information barriers.
Understand how information barriers help organizations determine which users to add or remove from a Microsoft Team, OneDrive account, and SharePoint site.
Describe how information barriers prevent users or groups from communicating and collaborating in Microsoft Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint.
keyPoints: IB applies to **Microsoft Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive** and supports only **two-way** restrictions — never one-way.
**Segments** group users by directory attributes such as Department; a user belongs to **one segment** and a segment gets **one policy**. Maximum **100 segments** per organization.
**Block** policies stop one segment talking to another; **Allow** policies let a segment talk only to listed segments. Microsoft recommends **Block** policies for most scenarios.
Define policies as **Inactive**, then set them **Active** and **apply** them; nothing affects users until then.
IB supports only **Microsoft 365 Groups**; distribution lists and security groups count as non-IB groups. Federated external users aren't restricted.
The **Information Barrier Policy Evaluation Service (IBPES)** checks Teams events (adding members, chats, meetings, screen sharing, calls) and re-evaluates existing chats when policies change.
Enable IB for SharePoint and OneDrive together with `Set-SPOTenant -InformationBarriersSuspension $false` (takes about an hour).
Explicit, Implicit, Inferred and Owner Moderated modes **disable Anyone and company-wide links**.

units.title: Explore Microsoft Purview Information Barriers
points: Used in highly regulated industries (e.g. FINRA guidance in financial services) to avoid conflicts of interest and insider trading.
Defined by a Compliance administrator or Information Barrier administrator.
In Teams, IB blocks searching for a user, adding members, starting chats, meeting invites, screen sharing, calls and file sharing.
In SharePoint and OneDrive, IB blocks adding members, accessing, sharing and searching sites or content.

units.title: Configure information barriers in Microsoft Purview
points: Configure in the Microsoft Purview portal (recommended for first-time setup) or Security & Compliance PowerShell.
Prerequisites: licenses and permissions, attribute data in the directory, Teams scoped directory search, audit logging on, **no Exchange address book policies**, admin consent for Teams.
Steps: prerequisites → segment users → define policies → apply → optionally configure SharePoint/OneDrive → optionally update IB modes.
Non-IB users are visible under Block policies but **hidden** under Allow policies unless included.
Hidden or disabled accounts can't communicate in IB-enabled organizations; their Teams chats are locked or they are removed.

units.title: Examine information barriers in Microsoft Teams
points: Blocked users don't appear in the people picker; blocked chats, meeting joins, screen shares and VoIP calls are refused. IB also applies to guests.
After a policy change: 1:1 chats become **read-only**; violating users are removed from group chats (old messages stay visible) and from teams.

Teams IB modes: **Open** (teams created before IB, no policies), **Implicit** (default for new teams), **Owner Moderated** (owner allows incompatible users). Move existing teams to Implicit with `Set-UnifiedGroup -InformationBarrierMode Implicit`.
Known issues: users can't join meetings once the chat roster is full, team members can't join channel meetings.

units.title: Examine information barriers in OneDrive
points: OneDrive modes: **Open** (non-segmented user), **Explicit** (segmented user; segment associated within 24 hours), **Owner Moderated** and **Inferred** (also share with unsegmented users; opt-in).
A OneDrive gets the user's segment plus compatible segments (up to 100); manage with `Set-SPOSite -AddInformationSegment` / `-RemoveInformationSegment`.
Adding a segment sets the mode to Explicit; removing all segments sets it to Open.
Owner Moderated requires no segments; Inferred requires segments.
A mismatch between a user's segment and their OneDrive's segments locks the user out of their own OneDrive.

units.title: Examine information barriers in SharePoint
points: Site modes: **Open** (no segments), **Owner Moderated** (only non-group-connected sites), **Implicit** (Teams-connected; access by Microsoft 365 group membership), **Explicit** (segments associated).
Explicit sites can be shared only with users whose segment matches; non-segmented users get an error.
Up to 100 **compatible** segments per site — incompatible segments (e.g. Sales and Research) can't share a site.
Sites created by a segmented user become Explicit with the user's segment; owners can add but not remove segments. Admin-created sites start Open.
Use `Set-SPOTenant -IBImplicitGroupBased $true` for group-membership-based control on Implicit sites (per geo in Multi-Geo).

keyTerms.definition: Group of users defined by a directory attribute and subject to the same IB policy.
IB policy that prevents one segment from communicating with another.
IB policy that lets a segment communicate only with specified segments.
Information Barrier Policy Evaluation Service — evaluates Teams events and existing memberships against IB policies.
Default IB mode for teams and Teams-connected sites created after IB is enabled; access follows group membership.
IB mode for sites or OneDrives with associated segments; only matching segments can access and be shared with.

tables.title: IB modes
rows: No segments / created before IB; no IB restrictions
Default for teams created after IB is enabled; group membership governs access
Segments associated with the site or OneDrive
Segmented OneDrive also shareable with unsegmented users (opt-in)

remember: Team A can't call team B but B may call A → **not possible**; IB is two-way only.
IB covers **Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive** — not Exchange email.
Existing teams after enabling IB stay **Open** → switch them to **Implicit**.
Need non-IB users to remain visible → use **Block**, not Allow, policies.

selfCheck.q: Investment bankers and financial advisors must never collaborate, but both work with HR. Which policy type and segments?
selfCheck.a: Segments for Investment bankers and Financial advisors (and HR), with Block policies between the two incompatible segments.

selfCheck.q: A user changes department and is now blocked from an existing 1:1 chat partner. What happens to the chat?
selfCheck.a: Further communication is blocked and the existing 1:1 chat becomes read-only.

selfCheck.q: You want an HR user's OneDrive to be accessible to HR and unsegmented users. Which mode?
selfCheck.a: Inferred, set with Set-SPOSite -InformationBarriersMode Inferred on a OneDrive that has segments.

modules.title: Explore Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention
modules.learnSummary: This module examines the data loss prevention features in Microsoft 365 that help organizations identify, monitor, report, and protect sensitive data through deep content analysis while helping users understand and manage data risks.
modules.tldr: Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) finds sensitive items through deep content analysis and protects them at rest, in use and in motion, across Microsoft 365, Office apps, endpoints, non-Microsoft cloud apps and on-premises repositories. Policies are made of rules (conditions plus actions) and should be tested in Simulation mode before you enforce them. Endpoint DLP extends this to Windows and macOS devices, and adaptive protection adjusts DLP and Conditional Access to each user's insider risk level.
objectives: Describe how Data Loss Prevention (DLP) is managed in Microsoft 365.
Understand how DLP in Microsoft 365 uses sensitive information types and search patterns.
Describe how Endpoint DLP extends the DLP activity monitoring and protection capabilities to devices.
Describe what a DLP policy is and what it contains.
Understand how adaptive protection integrates Insider Risk Management with DLP.
View DLP policy results using both queries and reports.
keyPoints: DLP uses **deep content analysis** — keywords, regular expressions, internal function validation and supporting evidence in proximity — plus machine learning, not simple text scans.
A DLP **policy** holds one or more **rules**; each rule has **conditions** (content and context) and **actions** (block, notify, policy tip, override).
Lifecycle: **plan** (technology, business processes, culture) → **prepare** (location prerequisites) → **deploy** (design, **Simulation mode**, tune, then **Enforce**).
Simulation runs up to **15 days**, keeps results **30 days**; *Stop processing more rules* doesn't work in Simulation mode. Policies take effect about an **hour** after being turned on.

**Endpoint DLP** covers onboarded Windows 10/11 and macOS devices (USB, network share, print, clipboard, cloud upload, Bluetooth, RDP); needs **E5 / A5** or the E5/A5 compliance or information protection and governance add-ons.
On-premises file shares need the **Microsoft Purview Information Protection scanner**; DLP policies can be scoped with **administrative units**.
**Adaptive protection** uses insider risk levels (**Elevated, Moderate, Minor**) to apply DLP and **Conditional Access** controls dynamically to high-risk users only.
Monitor results in the **DLP Alerts dashboard**, **Activity explorer** (last 30 days, filter **DLPRuleMatch**) and the **DLP Overview** page.

units.title: Examine data loss prevention for workloads
points: Reasons for DLP: compliance, reputation, IP protection, cost savings.
Protective actions: policy tip, block with override and justification, block without override, quarantine items at rest, hide sensitive info in Teams chat.
Plan business processes with process owners, deploy in test mode and evaluate in Activity explorer; use policy tips to raise awareness before enforcement.
Tune locations, scope, conditions, exceptions, sensitive info definitions, actions and restricted apps/sites while in Simulation mode.

units.title: Examine DLP policies
points: Conditions: content contains 80+ built-in sensitive info types, shared inside/outside the org, document properties (e.g. FCI).
Block access on site content restricts the item to the primary site collection admin, document owner and last modifier; blocked email gives an NDR or a policy tip.
Policy configuration: what to monitor (template or custom) → admin scoping (administrative units) → locations → conditions → actions.
Locations include Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, devices, Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps instances, on-premises repositories and Power BI.
Simulation mode evaluates all existing and new items in SharePoint/OneDrive, but only **new** items in Exchange, Teams and devices.

units.title: Explore Endpoint data loss prevention
points: Policy evaluation is central — no per-device distribution lag; updates sync in about an hour.
Auditable and restrictable: cloud upload/unallowed browsers (redirect to Microsoft Edge), copy to app, USB, network share, print; RDP and Bluetooth on Windows only. Create and rename are audit-only.
*Always audit file activity for devices* audits Office, PDF and .csv files even without a policy match.
File types and file extensions can't be combined as conditions in the same rule.
Onboard via local script (up to 10 devices), Group Policy, Configuration Manager, Intune or VDI scripts; Defender for Endpoint-onboarded devices appear automatically.

units.title: Explore adaptive protection in Microsoft Purview
points: Machine-learning-driven: context-aware detection, dynamic controls, automated mitigation.
Risk levels are based on **insights** (aggregated activity and severity), not raw activity counts.
Example controls: policy tips for Minor/Moderate users, block sharing for Elevated users; Conditional Access can require Terms of Use or block apps.
**Quick setup** creates an insider risk Data leaks policy, two DLP policies (Endpoint; Teams and Exchange) in test mode and a report-only Conditional Access policy; up to 72 hours to take effect.
**Custom setup** suits organizations that already have insider risk or DLP policies.

units.title: View DLP policy results
points: Reporting categories: Policy, Classification, Activity, Audit; reports export as CSV.
DLP data flows into the audit log first, then into the reporting tools.
DLP Alerts dashboard: configure, review, triage and track alerts with event metadata.
DLP Overview: unprotected sensitive documents in SharePoint/OneDrive, extending email DLP to auto-labeling, and automatic file protection in Teams.

keyTerms.definition: Part of a DLP policy consisting of conditions and the actions taken when they match.
Runs a DLP policy as if enforced, without actions, with results in a separate dashboard.
In-app notification warning a user that an action conflicts with a DLP policy, optionally allowing override.
Extends DLP monitoring and protection to onboarded Windows 10/11 and macOS devices.
Applies DLP and Conditional Access controls dynamically based on users' insider risk levels.
Default Activity explorer activity filter for DLP events.

tables.title: Adaptive protection risk levels (built-in definitions)
rows: High severity alerts, 3+ high severity sequence insights, or confirmed high severity alerts
Block saving/sharing sensitive data; block app access
Medium severity alerts or 2+ high severity exfiltration activities
Low severity alerts or 1+ high severity exfiltration activity
Policy tips; accept Terms of Use

remember: DLP policy contains **rules**; rules contain conditions and actions.
New policy → **Simulation mode** first, then Enforce.
On-premises file share DLP → needs the **information protection scanner**; Endpoint DLP → devices must be **onboarded**.
Adaptive protection = Insider Risk Management + DLP + **Conditional Access**.

selfCheck.q: Finance must be prevented from copying files with credit card numbers to USB drives. What do you configure?
selfCheck.a: An Endpoint DLP policy scoped to the Finance users' devices, with a rule detecting the Credit Card Number sensitive info type and the action set to Block.

selfCheck.q: A production DLP policy throws too many false positives. How do you test fixes safely?
selfCheck.a: Copy the policy, tune the copy and run it in Simulation mode; when results are good, turn off the old policy and enforce the new one.

selfCheck.q: You want only high-risk insiders blocked from sharing sensitive data while others just see tips. Which feature?
selfCheck.a: Adaptive protection, which maps insider risk levels to DLP (and Conditional Access) controls.

modules.title: Implement Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention
modules.learnSummary: This module examines how organizations can use Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention to help protect sensitive data and define the protective actions that organizations can take when a DLP rule is violated. MS-102
modules.tldr: Implementing Microsoft Purview DLP starts with planning: involve stakeholders, describe the sensitive data, agree on how much leakage you can tolerate, and roll out in stages from test mode to full enforcement. You can begin with the default DLP policies, then design custom policies around a written policy intent statement and build them from one of 40+ templates. Email notifications and policy tips (with override and false-positive reporting) teach users without stopping their work.
objectives: Create a data loss prevention implementation plan. Implement Microsoft 365's default DLP policy.
Create a custom DLP policy from a DLP template and from scratch.
Create email notifications and policy tips for users when a DLP rule applies.
Create policy tips for users when a DLP rule applies
Configure email notifications for DLP policies
keyPoints: Planning order: **identify stakeholders** → describe sensitive information categories → **set goals** → implementation plan. DLP needs are roughly **85% regulatory/compliance** and 15% IP protection.
Decide on **leakage tolerance** with the business — zero leakage can break processes; use exceptions or audit-only mode instead.
Recommended rollout: **test mode without policy tips** → **test mode with notifications and tips** → **full enforcement**. Rules can be turned off and reordered by priority on their own.

Two **default policies** exist before you create any: **Default policy for devices** (external sharing of sensitive content, refine from the Purview Home tile) and **Default policy for Teams** (alerts, no policy tips).
Write a one-sentence **policy intent statement** and map it to what/where/conditions/actions before building the policy.
Creating DLP policies needs the **DLP Compliance Management** role (View-Only DLP Compliance Management for read-only).
Email notifications: **individual internal recipients only**, triggered only by **new content**, HTML and tokens allowed (5,000 characters). Policy tip custom text: **plain text, 256 characters**.
Override is only available when the rule **blocks**; with several matching rules, only the **most restrictive** rule's tip is shown.

units.title: Plan to implement Microsoft Purview Data Loss Protection
points: Many starting points: platform focus, known sensitive data, discovery first, or straight to policies and refine.
Stakeholders: compliance officers, chief risk officer, legal, security, business data owners, business users and IT — IT shouldn't plan alone.
Policy planning questions: which regulations, which sensitive items, where are they and which processes use them, what is the leakage tolerance.
Example approaches: a regulated bank builds a labeling scheme methodically; a small startup uses the Teams default policy, blocks external sharing and blocks uploads to non-OneDrive cloud storage.
Review DLP requirements regularly as regulations and business goals change.

units.title: Implement Microsoft Purview's default DLP policies
points: Default policy for devices detects external sharing of content with credit card numbers, source code, U.S. HIPAA Enhanced matches or IP-related trainable classifier matches.
Refine it to send incident reports to admins or block with user override; it's fully customizable and can be turned off or deleted.
Default policy for Teams covers chat and channel (including private channel) messages, is on for all users, shows no policy tips and sends a low-severity alert email to an admin you add.
Rule matches can take up to 48 hours to show; the *Further protect shared content* widget only appears when no DLP policies exist.

units.title: Design a custom DLP policy
points: Avoid tuning by trial and error; document business needs in an intent statement and map each segment to configuration points.
Example: detect HIPAA data in OneDrive/SharePoint → HIPAA template, OneDrive/SharePoint/Teams locations, restrict access or encrypt action.
The chosen locations affect which conditions (sensitive info types, sensitivity labels, retention labels) and actions are available.
Renaming policies and rules is supported (preview); old records keep the old name, so agree a naming convention up front.

units.title: Create a custom DLP policy from a template
points: 40+ templates; tune them by adding sensitive info types, changing instance counts, allowing override with justification or changing notification recipients. The **Custom** template has no rules.
Grant access by creating a role group with **DLP Compliance Management** and adding a Microsoft 365 group of compliance officers.

Wizard: template → name → locations (on/off, include/exclude; site policies cover subsites) → default or advanced rules → info to protect → actions → access/override → policy mode (on, test, off) → review.
Information Protection roles (Admin, Analyst, Investigator, Reader) allow finer access control.

units.title: Configure email notifications for DLP policies
points: Turn on **User notifications** in a rule: policy tips on endpoints and in Microsoft 365 services, plus email notifications.
Recipients can be the content owner, last modifier, site owner or a specific user — not groups; external senders aren't notified; emails are sent unprotected.
Default subjects start with the action, e.g. *Message Blocked* or *Access Blocked*; message notifications attach the matching email.
Custom notifications support HTML and tokens: `%%AppliedActions%%`, `%%ContentURL%%`, `%%MatchedConditions%%`.

units.title: Configure policy tips for DLP policies
points: Policy tips can allow override with business justification or false-positive reporting; both are logged in DLP reports.
Override applies per rule and overrides all actions except *send a notification*; overriding the most restrictive rule overrides other matched rules too.
Outlook: tip above recipients while composing (body, subject or attachment); not shown for Microsoft Purview Message Encryption mail when the policy uses the detect encryption condition.
Policy tips come from **either** the Exchange admin center **or** Microsoft Purview, not both; email notifications are always sent.
Office desktop apps scan documents themselves; users can hide notify-only tips, but block/override tips still show.

keyTerms.definition: One-sentence summary of a DLP policy's business purpose, mapped to what, where, conditions and actions.
The agreed acceptable level of sensitive item sharing, expressed through thresholds such as instance counts.
Built-in DLP policy tracking sensitive info in Teams messages; alerts admins, no user policy tips.
Role required to create and manage DLP policies in Microsoft Purview.
Lets a user bypass a blocking rule, optionally with business justification or a false-positive report.

tables.title: Email notification vs. policy tip customization
rows: Triggered by edits to existing content
Individual internal users (no groups, no external senders)

remember: Users can't override → check the rule actually **blocks**; Notify-only rules never offer override.
Purview policy tips not showing in Outlook → tips configured in the **Exchange admin center** take precedence.
Stakeholders and sensitive data identified → next step is to **set protection goals**.
Rollout order: test **without** tips → test **with** tips → enforce.

selfCheck.q: Internal auditors must share some credit card numbers with external auditors, but security wants zero leakage. How do you resolve it?
selfCheck.a: Agree on an acceptable leakage level with the business, then add exceptions for those individuals or run the policy in audit-only mode.

selfCheck.q: A user should be able to bypass a block on sharing personal data internally, but must explain why. Which rule configuration?
selfCheck.a: Notify + Block + Allow Override + With justification.

selfCheck.q: Compliance officers need to create DLP policies without becoming global admins. What do you set up?
selfCheck.a: A role group in Microsoft Purview with the DLP Compliance Management role, with a Microsoft 365 group of the officers as members.

paths.title: MS-102 Manage compliance in Microsoft 365
paths.summary: This learning path provides instruction on managing the Microsoft 365 data governance features, including how to implement retention in email, sensitivity labels, and Windows Information Protection, and how to troubleshoot data loss prevention issues.

modules.title: Implement data classification of sensitive information
modules.learnSummary: This module introduces you to data classification in Microsoft 365, including how to create and train classifiers, view sensitive data using Content explorer and Activity explorer, and implement Document Fingerprinting.
modules.tldr: Data classification means identifying, categorizing and protecting content according to its sensitivity, ideally guided by a simple framework of 3–5 levels with clear controls. In Microsoft Purview you classify with sensitive information types, exact data match, trainable classifiers and Document Fingerprinting. Content explorer shows what is classified and where, and Activity explorer shows what users do with it.
objectives: Explain the benefits and pain points of creating a data classification framework.
Identify how data classification of sensitive items is handled in Microsoft 365.
Understand how Microsoft 365 uses trainable classifiers to protect sensitive data.
Create and then retrain custom trainable classifiers.
Analyze the results of your data classification efforts in Content explorer and Activity explorer.
Implement Document Fingerprinting to protect sensitive information being sent through Exchange Online.
keyPoints: A classification framework has **3–5 levels** (name, description, examples) plus **controls** per level; Microsoft recommends at most **5 parent labels × 5 sublabels**, with self-descriptive names.

Best practices: **crawl-walk-run**, write for a broad audience, go granular only if needed, involve senior and legal/privacy stakeholders, balance security against convenience. About **50%** of an information protection project is business-focused.
Classification starts with **zero change management**: content is scanned for sensitive and labeled items before you create any policies.

Classifier types: **sensitive info types** (patterns, keywords, proximity, confidence), **EDM** (exact values from a database, up to 100 million rows, fewer false positives) and **trainable classifiers** (learn from examples).

Custom trainable classifier: **50–500 seed** items → at least **200 test** items (max 10,000) → review **200+** predictions → **publish**. Classifiers work only on **unencrypted** items; pretrained classifiers can't be retrained.
Retraining starts automatically after **30 feedback** items (match / not a match) in Content explorer, takes 1–4 hours, and can run **twice a day**.
**Content explorer** needs the **list viewer** and/or **content viewer** role groups (not cumulative); **Activity explorer** shows up to **30 days** from the unified audit log.
**Document Fingerprinting** turns a standard form into a sensitive info type (stored as a hash); it's created only in **Security & Compliance PowerShell** and detects only in **Exchange Online**.

units.title: Explore data classification
points: Classify with sensitivity labels, retention labels, sensitive info types and trainable classifiers.
Typical levels: Public, Internal (Microsoft switched to *General*), Confidential, Highly Confidential; each level defines controls such as encryption, storage, access and DLP.
**Handling guidelines** tell users how to treat each level in daily work; a framework defines *what*, guidelines define *how*.
Pain points include designing levels, implementation planning, governance, KPIs, awareness and user training.
Ongoing governance: a governance body, defined roles, KPIs, tracking regulatory changes and standard operating procedures.

units.title: Implement data classification in Microsoft 365
points: The **Data classification** area shows top sensitive info types, top sensitivity and retention labels, user activity and data locations.
Labels can be applied manually, by default through policy, or automatically on a condition.
Small organizations may map one classification level to one sensitivity label; global organizations often can't, because a level may differ by region.
Pilot the taxonomy and adjust from feedback (Microsoft renamed *Personal* to *non-business*).

units.title: Explore trainable classifiers
points: Three ways to classify: manual, automated pattern matching (KQL, sensitive info types, fingerprinting, EDM) and trainable classifiers.
Classifiers identify an item by **what it is**, not by elements inside it; usable in sensitivity auto-labeling, retention label auto-apply and communication compliance.
Pretrained examples: Agreements, Finance, HR, IP, Resumes, Source Code, Tax, Harassment, Profanity, Threat, Customer Complaints.
