First-time opt-in by a Global Administrator; baseline evaluation takes about 12 days, and scanning 7–14 days.

units.title: Create and retrain a trainable classifier
points: Put seed and test content in **dedicated** SharePoint folders; allow an hour for indexing of new locations.
Requires Compliance administrator or Security administrator; seed processing takes up to 24 hours (status **Need test items**), test processing up to an hour (**Ready to review**).
Review predictions in batches of 30; once accuracy stabilizes the status becomes **Ready to use** and you can publish.
Retrain from Content explorer by giving feedback; giving feedback on **close matches** improves precision the most. Feedback stays in your tenant.
After retraining, compare versions and **Republish**, or keep the current version.

units.title: View sensitive data using Content explorer and Activity explorer
points: Requires E5-level licensing (e.g. Microsoft 365 E5/A5/G5, E5 Compliance, Office 365 E5).
Content explorer: a snapshot of labeled and classified items; its permissions override item permissions. Counts can take up to seven days to update; export to .csv.
Sensitivity labels must be enabled for SharePoint and OneDrive files for that data to surface.
Activity explorer: 30+ filters, label applied/changed/removed, auto-labeling simulation, DLP matches and Endpoint DLP file activities; doesn't monitor Exchange Online retention activities.
Activity explorer access: Information Protection roles or groups, Global, Compliance, Security or Compliance data administrator.

units.title: Detect sensitive information documents using Document Fingerprinting
points: Upload a blank standard form (patent, HIPAA, HR form); DLP turns its word pattern into a hash-based fingerprint — the original document isn't stored.
Not detected: password-protected files, image-only files, documents missing any of the original form text, or files over 10 MB; .dotx isn't supported.
Create with `New-DlpFingerprint` and `New-DlpSensitiveInformationType` in the **same** PowerShell session, then use it in a DLP rule (`New-DlpComplianceRule`) or a mail flow rule.
Allow exceptions (e.g. legal department) or override with justification.

keyTerms.definition: Enterprise policy defining 3–5 sensitivity levels with descriptions, examples and required controls.
Pattern-based classifier using patterns, keyword evidence, proximity and confidence levels.
Custom SIT that matches exact values from a refreshable database of sensitive records.
Machine-learning classifier that recognizes a content category from examples.
50–500 strong positive samples used to build a custom classifier's model.
DLP feature that converts a standard form into a sensitive info type for Exchange Online detection.

tables.title: Classification methods
rows: Credit card, bank account, national ID numbers
Exact values from an uploaded database
Structured records (employees, patients, customers) with few false positives
Content categories like contracts, resumes, source code
Word pattern of a standard form
Filled-in templates sent through Exchange Online

remember: Classifier doesn't recognize encrypted files → classifiers only work on **unencrypted** items.
Seeing a file *list* vs. seeing file *contents* in Content explorer → **list viewer** vs. **content viewer**; you need both for both.
Document Fingerprinting → **PowerShell only**, **Exchange Online only**.
Pretrained classifiers → **can't be retrained**; only custom ones can.

selfCheck.q: You must detect outbound emails that contain your company's filled-in patent application form. Which feature?
selfCheck.a: Document Fingerprinting: create a fingerprint of the blank form with New-DlpFingerprint, make it a sensitive info type and use it in a DLP policy.

selfCheck.q: A custom classifier misclassifies some contracts. How do you improve it?
selfCheck.a: Give match / not-a-match feedback in Content explorer (especially on close matches); after 30 items it retrains automatically, then review and republish.

selfCheck.q: An HR analyst must see which files contain sensitive data and where, but not open them. What do you grant?
selfCheck.a: Membership in the Content Explorer list viewer role group only.

modules.title: Explore sensitivity labels
modules.learnSummary: This module examines how sensitivity labels from the Microsoft Information Protection solution let you classify and protect your organization's data, while making sure that user productivity and collaboration isn't hindered.
modules.tldr: Sensitivity labels classify documents, emails, meetings and containers, and can protect them with encryption, content markings and container settings without getting in the way of collaboration. A label's scope decides where it appears, its position in the list decides its priority, and it can be applied manually, by default, by recommendation or automatically. Label policies publish labels to users and groups and add settings such as a default label, mandatory labeling and justification for downgrades.
objectives: Describe how sensitivity labels let you classify and protect your organization's data
Identify the common reasons why organizations use sensitivity labels
Explain what a sensitivity label is and what they can do for an organization
Configure a sensitivity label's scope
Explain why the order of sensitivity labels in your admin center is important
Describe what label policies can do
keyPoints: A sensitivity label is **customizable**, stored in **clear text** in metadata and **persistent** — it roams with the content. An item has **one sensitivity label** (plus one retention label).
Labels can **encrypt**, add **content markings** (header, footer, watermark — no watermarks on email), protect **containers** (Teams, groups, sites) or simply classify without protection.
**Scope** (Items: files, emails, meetings; Groups & sites; Schematized data assets) decides which settings you can configure and **where users see** the label.
**Order matters**: least restrictive at the top, most restrictive at the **bottom**; lower position = higher sensitivity, used for downgrade justification and auto-labeling conflicts.
**Sublabels** only group labels; they **don't inherit** parent settings, and a parent with sublabels can't be applied to content.

**Client-side** auto-labeling (Office apps) can recommend or apply as users work; **service-side** auto-labeling policies label data at rest in SharePoint/OneDrive and email in transit, and must run in **simulation** first.
**Label policies** publish to users and groups: default label, justification for downgrade or removal, mandatory labeling, custom help link. Changes take up to **24 hours**.
When a user has several label policies, the **highest-priority policy (lowest position)** wins for each conflicting setting.

units.title: Manage data protection using sensitivity labels
points: Labels are applied by users, by admin-defined automatic policies, or recommended by Microsoft 365 based on content.
Use cases: encryption and markings, protection in Office apps on all platforms, third-party apps via Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, container protection, classification only.
Labels extend to Power BI, Microsoft Purview Data Map assets and third-party apps using the Microsoft Purview Information Protection SDK.
Encryption can also restrict what authorized people can do with the content.

units.title: Explore what sensitivity labels can do
points: Encryption: admin-defined permissions per user/group and duration, or let users assign permissions when applying the label.
Marking limits: watermark 255 characters, header/footer 1,024 (Excel 255 total including formatting codes); some apps support dynamic markings with variables.
Container settings control privacy, external access and sharing, and access from unmanaged devices — they don't label the files inside.
Word, Excel and PowerPoint apply marking and encryption immediately; Outlook applies markings after Exchange Online sends the email.
Labels applied outside Office apps (scanner, SharePoint/OneDrive auto-labeling, Defender for Cloud Apps) add metadata and encryption but no content markings.

units.title: Determine a sensitivity label's scope
points: **Items** is always selected by default; Groups & sites and Schematized data assets are selected once those features are enabled for the tenant.
Settings pages for unselected scopes appear but can't be configured.
With multiple automatic or recommended matches, the **last** label (and last sublabel) wins; a sublabel set to automatic beats one set to recommended.
Deleting a label doesn't remove it from content — protection keeps being enforced; edited labels enforce the version that was applied.

units.title: Apply sensitivity labels automatically
points: Benefits: no need to train users on every classification or rely on them labeling correctly.
SharePoint/OneDrive limits: .docx/.pptx/.xlsx only, no open files, 25,000 auto-labeled files per day, 100 policies per tenant with up to 100 named sites each; modified dates aren't changed.
Exchange: scans PDF and Office attachments but labels only the email; label encryption overrides IRM from mail flow rules or DLP; incoming external mail isn't encrypted by default.
Auto-labeling doesn't replace manual labels or higher-sensitivity labels.
Simulation is mandatory before enforcement, takes up to 12 hours and supports up to 1,000,000 matched files.

units.title: Explore sensitivity label policies
points: Sensitivity labels are published to **users and groups** (retention labels to locations).
Avoid a default label that **encrypts** documents — it can block sharing with external users.
Mandatory labeling forces a label before saving, sending or creating a group/site; justification is logged in Activity explorer.
No label limit except **500 labels that apply encryption**; keep to about five main labels with five sublabels each.

keyTerms.definition: Persistent, clear-text metadata tag that classifies and can protect content or containers.
Determines the configurable settings and where a label is visible: items, groups & sites, or schematized data assets.
Label grouped under a parent for display; inherits nothing from the parent.
Service-side policy labeling SharePoint/OneDrive files at rest and Exchange email in transit; runs in simulation first.
Publishes labels to users and groups with settings like default label and mandatory labeling.
Requires users to apply a label before saving documents, sending email or creating groups/sites.

tables.title: Client-side vs. service-side auto-labeling
rows: Office apps while editing or composing
SharePoint/OneDrive at rest, Exchange email in transit

remember: Most restrictive label → **bottom** of the list; for label **policies**, the bottom policy has the **highest priority**.
Sensitivity labels publish to **users/groups**; retention labels publish to **locations**.
Watermarks → documents only, **not email**.
Deleting a label → existing content **keeps** its protection.

selfCheck.q: A label should only be available for Teams and SharePoint sites, not for documents. What do you configure?
selfCheck.a: The label's scope: select Groups & sites and clear the Items scope.

selfCheck.q: A user is in two label policies with different default labels. Which default applies?
selfCheck.a: The one from the policy with the highest priority, which is the policy lowest in the list.

selfCheck.q: You want to label thousands of existing Word files in SharePoint without depending on users' Office versions. What do you use?
selfCheck.a: A service-side auto-labeling policy for SharePoint/OneDrive, run in simulation mode first and then turned on.

modules.title: Implement sensitivity labels
modules.learnSummary: This module examines the process for implementing sensitivity labels, including applying proper administrative permissions, determining a deployment strategy, creating, configuring, and publishing labels, and removing and deleting labels.
modules.tldr: Roll out sensitivity labels in small iterations: create the labels, define what each one does, then publish them through label policies. First enable sensitivity labels for Office files in SharePoint and OneDrive, so the services can process encrypted files for co-authoring, search, eDiscovery and DLP. Removing a label from a policy can be undone, but deleting a label is not, and what happens to labeled content depends on where it is stored.
objectives: Create a deployment strategy for implementing sensitivity labels that satisfies your organization's requirements.
Enable sensitivity labels in SharePoint Online and OneDrive so they can use encrypted files.
Create and configure sensitivity labels.
Publish sensitivity labels by creating a label policy.
Identify the differences between removing and deleting sensitivity labels.
keyPoints: Deploy **iteratively**: handle one or two high-impact scenarios, create labels, validate, adjust, then move on; a project team owns requirements, proof of concept and approvals.
Three admin steps: **create** labels (named after your taxonomy) → **define what each label does** (protection settings) → **publish** with a label policy.

Enable labels for SharePoint and OneDrive so the services can **process encrypted files**: co-authoring, Office for the web, search, eDiscovery and DLP. Not supported for **HYOK** or **Double Key Encryption**.
Enable in the Microsoft Purview portal (Global Administrator) or with `Set-SPOTenant -EnableAIPIntegration $true` (required for **Multi-Geo**); takes about 15 minutes.
Delegate label admin through the **Information Protection** role groups or the **Sensitivity Label Administrator** role (Sensitivity Label Reader for read-only); applying labels needs no admin role.
Editing a published label needs **no republish**; allow **24 hours** (up to 48 for group-dependent changes). Keep as **few label policies** as possible — often just one.
When publishing a **sublabel**, also select its **parent** label.

**Remove from policy** = label disappears from apps but stays on content (reversible). **Delete** = archived protection template, no label name shown, and encryption removed for SharePoint/OneDrive files that the service can process.

units.title: Plan your deployment strategy for sensitivity labels
points: Scenarios: label Office content, encrypt documents and email, label in Office for the web, co-author encrypted files, auto-label, protect Teams/SharePoint containers, set default sharing links.
Labels also work as DLP conditions, as a trigger for retention labels, with the on-premises scanner, Defender for Cloud Apps, SQL columns, Power BI and Purview Data Map assets.
The best end-user documentation is your own, linked through the label policy's **custom help page** setting.
Encrypted PDFs can be opened in Microsoft Edge on Windows or Mac.

units.title: Enable sensitivity labels for files in SharePoint and OneDrive
points: Two reasons: users can apply labels in Office for the web, and SharePoint/OneDrive can process encrypted Office and PDF content.
Uploaders need at least **View** usage rights, otherwise the label isn't recognized; guests can open encrypted documents with guest accounts.
Existing encrypted files only benefit after being re-uploaded or edited.
New audit events: applied, changed and removed sensitivity label on a file.
Optional PDF support can increase auto-labeling volume (limit 25,000 files per day); the setting can be disabled at any time.

units.title: Examine the requirements to create a sensitivity label
points: Start with simple names (Personal, Public, General, Confidential, Highly Confidential) and use tooltips and sublabels.
Match protection to sensitivity: e.g. a footer for General, watermark plus encryption for Highly Confidential.
A label is defined once and reused across policies — pilot with a small policy, then create one for all users.
Licensing depends on the features you use.

units.title: Create sensitivity labels
points: Tenants have no labels by default; create them under **Information protection > Labels**.
Wizard: name, display name, user and admin descriptions → scope (Files & emails, Groups & sites, Schematized data assets) → settings for each scope.
Create sublabels via **Actions > Add sub label**; review the order with Move up / Move down.
Use **Publish label** only when you really need a new label policy.

units.title: Publish sensitivity labels
points: **Label policies > Publish label** starts the wizard: choose labels, then policy settings matching the labels' scopes.
Group/site settings (default label, mandatory label) only appear when the chosen labels include the Groups & sites scope.
Create separate policies for different users or settings, and order them to resolve conflicts.
There's no republish action — editing a policy replicates automatically; new labels can appear in Office for the web within the hour.

units.title: Remove and delete sensitivity labels
points: You can't delete a label that is still in a label policy.
Removed labels stay on content and container labels keep protecting sites.
Deleting an encrypting label archives its protection template, so you can't reuse the label name.
Outside SharePoint/OneDrive (or without the feature enabled) the label metadata and encryption remain, but no label name is shown.
Container settings stop being enforced, typically within 48–72 hours for SharePoint sites.

keyTerms.definition: Publishes selected labels and settings to chosen users and groups; editing it needs no republish.
Set-SPOTenant parameter that enables sensitivity labels for Office files in SharePoint and OneDrive.
Encryption template behind an encrypting label; archived (not deleted) when the label is deleted.
Encryption with an organization-held key; SharePoint/OneDrive can't process content encrypted this way.
Role for creating and managing labels without full tenant admin rights.

tables.title: Remove from policy vs. delete a label
rows: Metadata may remain, but no name is displayed
Template archived; removed for processable SharePoint/OneDrive files, kept elsewhere
No longer enforced (48–72 hours for SharePoint)

remember: Labels created and named → next step is to **define their protection settings**, then publish.
Edited a published label → **no extra steps**, just wait up to 24 hours.
Multi-Geo tenant → enable SharePoint/OneDrive labeling with **PowerShell per geo**.
Co-authoring/search not working on encrypted files → enable labels for SharePoint and OneDrive (unless DKE/HYOK is used).

selfCheck.q: Users can't co-author or search Word files encrypted by a label in SharePoint. What's missing?
selfCheck.a: Sensitivity labels for Office files in SharePoint and OneDrive haven't been enabled (e.g. Set-SPOTenant -EnableAIPIntegration $true).

selfCheck.q: During testing you no longer want users to see a label but might need it later. Remove or delete?
selfCheck.a: Remove it from the label policy — this can be undone and doesn't affect content already labeled.

selfCheck.q: A user opens a locally stored, encrypted file whose label was deleted. What do they see?
selfCheck.a: No label name, but the encryption remains and they see the archived protection template's name and description.
